articles.title: Canadian citizen detained at U.S. border crossing, questioned about voting for hours

image.caption: Paige Adamson says she was detained until nearly 3 a.m. PT and was 'basically treated like a criminal' when she attempted to cross the Canada-U.S. border at the Point Roberts border crossing on Sept. 15. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Paige Adamson was on her way home from a birthday dinner in Tsawwassen, B.C., on Sept. 15 when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing and questioned about voting for hours. Lawyers are raising concerns around vulnerabilities Canadians face while living in the U.S., especially over being registered to vote.
'Tip of the iceberg': One lawyer warns more Canadians could be detained over illegal voting concerns
Paige Adamson was on her way home from a birthday dinner in Tsawwassen, B.C., on Sept. 15 when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing.
It was a regular stop that Adamson — a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years — had grown used to.
But this time, they had a new question for her.
"The very first thing she asked was, 'Have you ever voted in a federal U.S. election?'" said Adamson.
Adamson, 61, said she told the border agent she had never voted in a federal election.
"They immediately said, 'Park over here and come into the office.'"

What happened next, Adamson said, was a nearly six-hour-long process — where she went through secondary inspection just after 9 p.m., was interrogated until after 2 a.m. and signed documents before being admitted into the U.S.
One of the documents CBC News reviewed said Adamson "must surrender for removal from the United States, if so ordered."

Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned in the last week.
Grounds for removal

According to documents provided by Adamson, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) alleges she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen "for the purposes of registering to vote in Whatcom County, Washington state."
The department also alleges Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election.
DHS cites those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S.

But Adamson maintained during questioning, a transcript reviewed by CBC News showed, that she has never voted in a federal election and doesn't remember ever voting in a state election — though she acknowledged receiving a ballot and may have been registered.
Adamson is now scheduled to appear for a hearing in Seattle, and is grappling with potentially being removed from the state she has lived in since 2012.
"My anxiety is over the top," she said.
A broader trend
In the past week and a half, immigration lawyer Len Saunders said he has received calls from three people — including Adamson — about being detained at the border and questioned about voting.
One, he said, was a Blaine, Wash., resident who crosses the border daily to work as a nurse in B.C.
Saunders said three near-identical situations like this in such a short period is unprecedented in his career that stretches back more than 25 years.
The Blaine-based lawyer told CBC News there could be hundreds of Canadians facing similar issues, and expects more cases as Canadians cross the border during the holidays.
"This is just the tip of the iceberg," he said.
B.C. immigration lawyer Chris Anders said border enforcement is "way, way stricter and tougher" than at any point in the last two decades.
He said the databases used by border officials are constantly expanding, meaning something that did not cause problems for someone previously could suddenly pop up during a new entry.
Voter registration issues
Washington state automatically registers some eligible voters when they get or renew a driver's licence or state ID, but the state says the system is tied to proof of U.S. citizenship.

But internal Washington Department of Licensing emails, obtained by the non-profit Federation for American Immigration Reform through a Freedom of Information request, show instances where non-citizens were registered to vote.
"A lot of Canadians say, 'Well, I thought I was entitled to [vote] because I went in, got my driver's licence and they registered me to vote,'" said Saunders.

items: Change in Canada's citizenship law hitting U.S. archives
Winnipeg-born man deported back to Canada after 9 months in ICE detention

blocks.text: Saunders said that in those situations, he has told clients to immediately deregister and submit a declaration saying they "unknowingly registered or unknowingly voted," and that used to be a consistent solution.
"Now, it seems to be a completely different scenario during this current administration."
The detainment

In an email to CBC News, a spokesperson for the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said when a permanent resident arrives at a port of entry, officers screen their documentation against federal and state databases.

The CBP says if those records indicate "potential unlawful voter registration, illegal voting, or a previous false claim to U.S. citizenship," the individual is subject to "rigorous examination and detailed questioning."
Depending on the case, an individual may face "prolonged" immigration inspections, receive a notice to appear and formal removal proceedings, the spokesperson said.
Are U.S. border agents allowed to search my phone? Your border questions answered
Adamson said she wasn't offered water until around the five-hour mark of her detainment, and no one asked whether she needed to use the bathroom.
"I was basically treated like a criminal," she said.
She said the large Canadian population in Point Roberts — an exclave of the U.S. located just south of Delta, B.C. — has left her concerned that some of her neighbours could face similar problems.
"This beautiful little place, it's kind of being invaded," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

articles.title: B.C. man uses motion-activated zombie to scare bears away from garbage
articles.summary: More than 33 bears have been killed by conservation officers in B.C. this year, including two that entered stores through automatic sliding doors in Hope and Squamish. It's led to creative solutions…

image.caption: Stephen Fryer's surveillance footage captured a bear being scared off by the motion-activated Halloween decoration, a creative solution being employed to scare the animals away as they seek food at lower elevations. (Submitted by Stephen Fryer)

blocks.text: British Columbia

More than 33 bears have been killed by conservation officers in B.C. this year, including two that entered stores through automatic sliding doors in Hope and Squamish. It's led to creative solutions to keep the hungry animals away from attractants.
The bears have been ripping off Stephen Fryer's bins, destroying the handles and lids
A Squamish, B.C., homeowner is using a motion-activated Halloween decoration to scare bears away from his garbage bins.
Stephen Fryer has been dealing with bears constantly in the Brackendale neighbourhood, about 50 kilometres north of Vancouver.
"They're around us every single day," Fryer said.

Officials say animals are looking for food at lower elevations, after drought and wildfires at higher elevations have reduced their food sources. Fryer is one homeowner who is trying a creative way to keep the bears out of his garbage.
He stores his bins outside, as he does not have a garage, and the bears often tip the bins to get inside.
"The garbage, the handles have been like chewed off — not ripped off, chewed off, because they're trying to get into it," Fryer said.
Fryer decided to reinforce the bins to the side of his house with a bolt and strap — but that didn't work either.
"One of them finally figured out how to rip it out of the wall and pulled the ... I-hook out of the wall and off the strap," Fryer said.
His wife had asked for the Halloween decorations to be set up in September, and that's when Fryer got an idea to put a motion-activated zombie on top of the garbage bins.
"It absolutely scared the bear to the point where it it peed itself," Fryer said.
Squamish man uses Halloween decorations to keep bears out of garbage
Surveillance video shows a burly black bear sniffing the bins. Moments later, the zombie lets out a scream and pops up.
"Another one came by, and it went off," Fryer said.

items: Bear killed by authorities after wandering through pharmacy with cub in Hope

blocks.text: Since the zombie was installed, the bears have been deterred.
"As funny as that is, it's totally worked," Fryer said.
More than 30 bears killed
In Squamish, 90 tickets have been issued in connection with the wildlife attractant bylaw, which includes leaving garbage out and not picking up fruit from fallen trees.
"The number of complaints we're getting is pretty high each day," said Sgt. Chris Doyle with the BCCOS's Sea-to-Sky zone.
The BCCOS said more bears are being seen at lower elevations.
"There's a lot less berries at higher elevations than there should be for a normal year, and that's likely driving a lot of the conflict," Doyle said.
Between January and July this year, conservation officers have responded to 13,672 calls regarding black bears in B.C.
At least 33 black bears have been killed in the first seven months of the year. September is often the deadliest month, with nine being killed last year.
Bears killed after entering stores
A bear wandered into a Squamish grocery store on Sept. 17 around 3 p.m. PT through automatic sliding doors.
Video captured the bear walking near the produce section of the store, and shortly after, it left through the sliding doors.
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) said the bear also entered another business in the downtown area.
When officers arrived, the bear was outside the store. Officers tranquillized the bear and killed it.
In a statement, the service said the bear was killed "due to public safety concerns".
A similar incident occurred in Hope recently when a black bear and its cub entered a pharmacy on Sept. 20 through automatic sliding doors.
BCCOS confirmed the mother bear was killed and the cub was released into a wilderness area.

"Bears that pose a serious threat to public safety, such as those that display a minimal fear of people or are conditioned to non-natural food sources, are not candidates for relocation or rehabilitation, as the risk is simply far too great," said the service.
Calls for change
Advocates argue that more can be done to prevent bears from being killed.
Holly Reisner with North Shore Black Bear Society said there has been an increased level of bear activity in B.C.
"These automated doors are just allowing bears to enter," Reisner said. "The bears are very attracted by any type of odour."
She's encouraging businesses to consider replacing the doors so bears cannot enter.
Lesley Fox, executive director of The Fur-Bearers, said a bear walking through a doorway should not be a death sentence.
"The question should be what the bear actually did, whether they posed a genuine threat, and whether reasonable non-lethal options were available," Fox said.

items: 'He could barely paddle anymore': B.C. family rescues bear cub from Okanagan Lake

blocks.text: She suggests better security features be installed.
"These are preventable problems," Fox said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alanna Kelly is a CBC News journalist based in Squamish, B.C., covering the Sea-to-Sky region, including Whistler, Pemberton and the Sunshine Coast. You can email story ideas to alanna.kelly@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris ahead of open-air Mass
articles.summary: More than half a million people are expected to attend the event in the heart of the French capital.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Hundreds of thousands of people have greeted Pope Leo XIV in the centre of Paris ahead of a giant open-air Mass.
Crowds cheered as the pontiff moved down the Champs-Élysées Avenue beneath the Arc de Triomphe, waving to crowds from his popemobile.
The head of the Catholic Church blessed several babies as he stopped at different stages along the avenue as chants of "Leo, Leo" rang out.
More than half a million people are expected to attend the event in the heart of the French capital on Saturday and a special altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde for the ceremony.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thousands have gathered along Champs-Elysees Avenue ahead of Pope Leo's open-air Mass

blocks.text: Thousands have gathered along Champs-Elysees Avenue ahead of Pope Leo's open-air Mass

French President Emmanuel Macron, who met Leo for an hour of talks on Friday, will not be at any of the Pope's Masses during his four-day visit to France, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.
But the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by Macron's wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also expected to attend.

Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally party and conservative Bruno Retailleau were both pictured at the Place de la Concorde ahead of the event, while centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal are also due to be there.
Mayor of Le Havre and former French Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and former Prime Minister Francois Fillon were both also seen at the Place de la Concorde.

blocks.caption: The pope moves through crowds in his popemobile. Several police officers can be seen nearby. Members of the crowd can be seen waving flags.

blocks.text: Earlier on Saturday, the Pope met migrants as he visited the Maison Bakhita centre, an association supporting refugees, and praised the organisation for inviting "us to see those who are invisible".
During the visit Leo said it was "possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace".
He also stressed the "the fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love".
The Pope also issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his visit to France on Friday.
Leo cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the Élysée Palace.
Why is the Pope in France?

blocks.caption: A cardboard cut out of Pope Leo is seen above the crowds at the Place de la Concorde

blocks.text: Large crowds are expected throughout the pontiff's trip, which the Church believes reflects a growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans.
On Sunday, 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes.

The Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, on Monday where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.
Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.

His paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later, she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden name.

articles.title: German Olympic Committee names Munich as bid city choice
articles.summary: Munich has been voted as the city that will bid for the Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044. Berlin had been in the running but withdrew on Thursday.

image.caption: Germany's entry will have to compete against other international cities to host the OlympicsImage: Franz Feiner/Eibner-Presse/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) on Saturday announced it chose Munich as Germany's entry to bid for at least the next three Olympic Summer Games.

Ahead of the vote, former Olympic champion and new Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said: "We have an international task to fulfill and must enter the race with the city or region that gives Germany the greatest chances internationally. The decision on that is made by sport, and I assume that it will make it with a great deal of responsibility."
Berlin bowing out created two-horse race
Munich and a Cologne-led bid by the Rhine-Ruhr region were the only two in contention.
As many as 17.6 million tickets could be sold for the Games in Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr, more than ever before at a Games, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia said recently.
Munich was campaigning after two failed bids for the 2018 and 2022 Winter Games and having previously hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.
Up until Thursday, Berlin had been among the cities in contention, but the city's mayor announced that the city would withdraw from the race.

The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in the German capital's elections last weekend. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.
Take a tour of Berlin's iconic Olympic Stadium
Sports minister has sights set on 2040
On Friday, Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said he would welcome a German Olympic bid for the 2040 Games, with it coinciding with an important historical milestone.

blocks.caption: Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said the city or region that gave Germany the greatest chances internationally should be voted forImage: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: "2040 will mark the 50th anniversary of reunification. Here we could send a great signal that also aligns with the values of the Olympic Games,” Rauhe told German news agency dpa ahead of the deciding vote on Saturday.

"Based on my personal history, 2040 would be my favorite date. That has to do with the fact that I'm a Berlin child. As a schoolchild, I experienced what happens to people when a wall falls, when people grow together again, when two population groups that had been separated become a community again,” Rauhe said.
"Ultimately, though, one thing matters above all: bringing the Olympic and Paralympic Games back to our country. No matter when," Rauhe said.

articles.title: DOLE launches skills certification program for TUPAD workers
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) on Saturday launched SkillPass, a skills certification program for Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) beneficiaries…

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 8:13pm

The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) on Saturday launched SkillPass, a skills certification program for Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) beneficiaries aimed at expanding their training and employment opportunities.
TUPAD is the agency’s community-based assistance package that provides temporary emergency employment for displaced, underemployed, and seasonal workers.

“A key TUPAD innovation is SkillPass, which helps beneficiaries turn their temporary work experience into a record of certifiable skills they can use for their next opportunity. It documents the work they performed and the competencies or certifications they earned,” DOLE said in a press release.

DOLE said that beneficiaries can use the competency credentials compiled in their SkillPass to apply for formal jobs, start a small business, seek employment overseas, or pursue further technical training.

“The beneficiary’s work and skills records will be consolidated into a SkillPass certification, issued within 15 days following their TUPAD engagement. Beneficiaries will then be referred to appropriate employment, livelihood, or skills training opportunities based on their qualifications and goal,” the agency said.
Program participants will also undergo profiling to determine the most suitable career, employment, or enterprise path for them.

This profiling and job-matching process will be carried out in coordination with various partners, including the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) and Public Employment Service Offices (PESO).

“Priority areas include digital services, green construction, agriculture and post-harvest activities, care work, food service, transport, equipment maintenance, and other nationally or locally in-demand occupations,” DOLE added.
Trabahong-Dagat
The Labor Department likewise introduced Trabahong-Dagat and Blue Enterprise Development on Saturday.
It is a work-to-skills employment and livelihood initiative for TUPAD workers, especially in coastal communities, initially rolling out in Zambales and the Zamboanga Peninsula.

The program is open to registered fisherfolk and their families, coastal youth, first-time jobseekers, and graduates of fisheries, maritime, or TESDA courses. It also extends to displaced or seasonal workers and members of legitimate fisherfolk organizations, labor unions, and cooperatives.
DOLE said the program will feature the following three tracks:

items: Dagat Skills and Services - maritime and fishing-related operations
Isda Skills and Production - aquaculture and fisheries development
Blue Enterprise Development - aimed at helping turn technical skills into viable small businesses

blocks.text: The Trabahong-Dagat and Blue Enterprise Development program will be implemented in collaboration with partner agencies, including the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, MARINA, PESOs, and the Philippine Coast Guard. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Propaganda in Russian schools prepares students to die
articles.summary: The Russian government wants children to learn about patriotism from an early age. DW spoke to students in Siberia about their views on propaganda, the war in Ukraine and their future.

image.caption: Patriotism has become a core part of the national curriculum since 2022Image: Konstanin Kokoshkin/Pivcario/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this year, several schools in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.6 million in southern Siberia, received a textbook on patriotism from the authorities. According to students, with whom DW spoke to on condition of anonymity, in the book the authors urge children to prepare themselves to die for their country. Furthermore, they equate homosexuality with pedophilia and Disney cartoons with pornography, and give instructions on how women should use their "charms." Europeans are described as "thieves, murderers and liars."

The textbook, which provides "materials for spiritual, moral, and patriotic upbringing" is supposed to be used as part of "patriotism lessons" that have been on the curriculum since 2022. Though it is not included on the national list of core curriculum books, the content reflects the Kremlin's intentions to spread propaganda in educational institutions.
'Love always involves sacrifice.'

One of the main topics of the book is the war in Ukraine and the idea that dying for one's country is a blessing is repeated several times: "Love always involves sacrifice," writes one of the authors. "The sacrifice of a defender of the homeland is their life."

Elsewhere in the book, the authors make constant claims that Russia is better than Western countries. They also say that children are "mentally crippled" because of "computer games, Hollywood action films, pornography and Disney cartoons."

They argue that European nations that used to be colonial empires legitimized "murder, lies and plunder" through the conquest and subjugation of new territories. Russia, on the other hand, "never exploited its numerous peoples," they say, but merely improved their living conditions. The book makes no mention of the culture of Indigenous peoples in what is Russia today, or of any religions other than Christianity and "Slavic paganism."

blocks.caption: This textbook is used in certain Russian schools to teach children about patriotism and other subjectsImage: M. Remaevich

blocks.text: 'More cannon fodder'

For Ilya, a 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk who has read the book and whose name has been changed, the idea of dying for his country is anathema. "It's proof that the country wants more cannon fodder," he told DW, adding that "dying for the country" actually meant dying for "the president's interests and ambitions."

He said that a few years ago, he had started watching the videos of Alexei Navalny, the Kremlin critic and opposition leader who died in jail in 2024 "more for fun than for any other reason." He said it was Navalny's 2021 investigation into Russian President Vladimir Putin's Black Sea palace that had first drawn his attention.

But it was when the authorities decided to block access to the US platforms YouTube and Discord that he began to oppose the government. He set up a VPN out of "contrariness" he said, looking for information about other opposition figures and reading the independent media. As he found out more about the cruelty and senselessness of the war, he criticized the government more strongly.

He confirmed that propaganda had become an integral part of the curriculum in the past four years. On top of the "Conversations about Important Things" that take place every Monday morning, there are now also subjects such as "Fundamentals of Homeland Security and Defense." He said that people who have taken part in the war in Ukraine are invited to lessons focusing on students' future and decisions regarding what career path to take.

Even outside of the classroom, students are encouraged to be "patriotic." Ilya said that a student had been reprimanded by the principal for wearing a sweater with a slogan written in English on it. "Young man, do you realize that your sweater has words on it in the language of unfriendly countries?" she reportedly asked him. "A call to the Federal Security Service will take care of that!"

Ilya also recalled that a school assembly held to mark May 9, which commemorates the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, the principal and her deputy had compared what is known in Russia as the "Great Patriotic War" to the current war in Ukraine. They had said that Russia would once again be steadfast and emerge victorious.

blocks.caption: Students are taught about being a soldier and told it is an honor to die for the country Image: Konstantin Kokoshkin/Picvario/Russian Look/Global Look Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'I love freedom'

Alexei (name changed), another 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk, told DW that many of his classmates avoided going to "patriotic events." He too said that the blocking of YouTube had made a difference to him. "I looked into why it was blocked," he said. "Because nothing happens by chance. And that's how my interest in politics began." That's when he realized that the authorities wanted to get rid of inconvenient citizens and suppress free speech. "I love freedom, so it was hard," he said.

Ilya thinks that most students don't take the propaganda seriously. "On the one hand, we laugh about it in class, at least my friends do," he said. "On the other, we don't care. Some simply don't listen. We're very good at being quiet and not talking much about it,"

Dima Zicer is an educator and the author of the Russian-language podcast "Love, Don't Discipline" who moved to Estonia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He told DW that "many students are happy to be part of a pro-Putin majority that doesn't think about things, according to the principle: 'We'll crush them all; we're stronger than everyone else. Everyone will be scared of us.'"

He said that there was no statistical data to back his argument, but he said that he had drawn his conclusions from his extensive experience working with Russian children, as well as his communication with parents. He said that these often only became aware of how serious the situation was when their children started saying things such as "We'll crush them" or "Putin is great," as well as talking about supposed Nazis and fascists in Ukraine.
Alexei and Ilya, who think differently and want the war in Ukraine to end, are worried about the unstable situation in Russia. They want to leave the country after graduating.
Protesting Putin: Russian opposition in exile
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: Paris: Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass before huge crowd
articles.summary: The pope addressed around 700,000 people during a Mass at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees. Leo XIV is on a four-day visit to France.

image.caption: Leo XIV traveled by popemobile to Paris' Place de la Concorde for the MassImage: Remo Casilli/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV on Saturday celebrated Mass for hundreds of thousands of worshippers in central Paris.
The Vatican said some 700,000 people were in attendance for the open-air service at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees.

blocks.caption: Around 600,000 people registered to attend the open-air mass with Pope Leo XIVImage: Gonzalo Fuentes/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the Mass?
The Mass began mid-afternoon after the pontiff traveled down the French capital's iconic avenue in his popemobile, cheered by the faithful lining the route.

News agencies described how the crowd stretched ‌2.2 kilometers(1.4 miles) across ⁠central ⁠Paris, with many waving white and yellow flags and pressing against security barriers for a glimpse of the pontiff.
At the Mass site, a huge white canopy was erected to serve as a makeshift altar for Leo to deliver his service.
Dozens of screens were installed to allow worshippers to follow the proceedings.
In his homily, Leo asked worshippers not to keep their faith to themselves

"Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied," he said. "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France."
Crowds began queuing hours before the service began, with many parents and children among those hoping to catch a glimpse of the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
"It's a big event; we've come to share the Christian fervour," teacher Sylvie Leclerc told the AFP news agency.
"You don't hear much from us Catholics, but now we're going to make some noise! But to proclaim love, peace, joy," she added.
Earlier on Saturday, the pope visited a social center and later met with adults who had recently been baptized.

blocks.caption: People began gathering hours before the start of the mass in central ParisImage: Gonzalo Fuentes/REUTERS

blocks.text: Leo's first trip to France as pope
Pope Leo is on a four-day visit to France that will see him travel to Lourdes and Metz, as well as Paris. It's his first visit to France since becoming pope last year.

On Friday, around 300,000 people gathered to see the pontiff as he waved from his popemobile on the way to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral, which had to be restored after a devastating fire in 2019.
French President Emmanuel Macron did not appear at the Mass. However, far-right leader Marine Le Pen and centrist Edouard Philippe have confirmed their attendance.

articles.title: UN adds 61 companies to settlements blacklist over alleged Palestinian human rights violations
articles.summary:
Human rights council names and shames businesses with ties to illegal Israeli settlements in West Bank

The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it…

blocks.text: The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are involved in violating Palestinian human rights through business ties to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The vast majority of the total 214 companies, which are based in 11 countries, are Israeli. Five of the 158 companies listed last year were removed in the latest update.

The blacklist, first published in 2020, was born of a vote by the UN’s human rights council, which has no ability to force companies to act. Its main goal is to name and shame businesses with ties to the settlements.
It is unclear how the inclusion on the list has affected the companies financially.

“This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses,” said Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, in a statement.

Israel said it “categorically rejects” the publication. “This database is meant to serve as a blacklist against businesses that have committed no wrongdoing,” the Israeli diplomatic mission in Geneva said in a statement. “We call on friends not to yield to this ugly attempt to blacklist Israeli firms.”
The UN office said it had advised the companies of their listing and given them a right of reply.
The latest report comes as Israeli settlements in Palestinian areas have faced new scrutiny.

Earlier this month, Britain banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, where it says “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. France and Canada announced they would take similar action.

articles.title: We followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell us
articles.summary:
Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear

What does it take to make a morning…

blocks.text: What does it take to make a morning cup of tea in Gaza?

For Alaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.

For 12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.

Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?

Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, when aid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.

blocks.caption: Ramadan on the beach at Al-Nuwairi, near Nuseirat, where he lives in a tent among the dunes. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Most of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.

There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.

There is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.
Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, deciding how many calories it will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.

Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans a plethora of ordinary objects from entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.

blocks.caption: Rajab al-Reefi, leader of Gaza Skate Team, helps other team-members to repair some boards. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: From the story of Rajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.

But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.

A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.

blocks.caption: Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem in front of the flat-bed truck that is now her home. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Still, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human. Prof Mahmoud Seydam wires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike. Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.
You can read all five of their days here.

articles.title: Teodoro on plans for 2028 polls: Who knows what will happen?
articles.summary: Teodoro on plans for 2028 polls: Who knows what will happen?

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 6:54pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro remains "undecided" on whether he will run for the 2028 presidential elections, as he was asked at the Saturday News Forum about President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s potential pick for the next polls.
“I’ll cross that bridge when I get there and I’ll weigh what’s best for the situation I find myself in," Teodoro said.
"I’ve been there and I’ve done that before... I ran for senator, didn’t make it. I find myself here. I find myself in this situation, so who knows what will happen?” he added.
Teodoro ran in the 2010 presidential elections and came in fourth place. He ran again as a senator in the 2022 elections but did not make the Magic 12.
While still unsure about his political plans, Teodoro stressed the importance of how the 2028 elections in terms of asserting the country's rights in the West Philippine Sea.

“Napaka-importante nito kasi ang quality of life and sustenance, hindi ngayon, dahil ang ating tinatanim ngayon, aanihin ito ng future generations, lalong-lalo na, kung titingnan natin, ang kalupaan ay nakaharap sa matinding hamon ng climate change, lindol, napakaraming mga hamon. Saan tayo pupunta?” Teodoro said.

(This is so important because it is a matter of quality of life and sustenance, not now, but we are planting the seeds that will be sowed by the future generations, especially now when our land has so many problems, from climate change, earthquakes, and so many challenges. Where would we go?)
Any slowdown in the assertion of rights over the West Philippine Sea could also result in a slowdown of the economy, Teodoro explained.

He also questioned what would happen to the economy if a leader would allow Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators (POGO) hub and undocumented tourists in the country. He also said that the proliferation of substandard goods could also ruin trade.

Teodoro said that it was not a matter of being willing to fight foreign powers over the West Philippine Sea, but a leader must be ready to resist influence. He said that the proper leader should be able to position the country towards a sustainable, law-based future. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: At long last, Mary Jane Veloso back home in Nueva Ecija
articles.summary: The moment that Mary Jane Veloso says she has fervently prayed for finally comes, following 16 long years of imprisonment

blocks.text: HOMECOMING. Mary Jane Veloso arrives in Nueva Ecija on September 26, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
The moment that Mary Jane Veloso says she has fervently prayed for finally comes, following 16 long years of imprisonment

items: Mary Jane Veloso came home to Nueva Ecija after her release from prison.
Before returning home, Veloso attended Mass with her family and held a press conference, where she expressed gratitude to the Lord, her family, and all her supporters.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
NUEVA ECIJA, Philippines – After 16 years in prison, Mary Jane Veloso returned home to her province of Nueva Ecija as a free woman on Saturday, September 26.

Her much-awaited homecoming came a day after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed he granted an absolute pardon to Veloso for the drug trafficking conviction handed down by an Indonesian court in 2010.
The release of the former overseas Filipino worker from the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City was formalized hours after Marcos’ announcement on Friday, September 25.
Veloso’s family immediately headed to Manila to greet her upon her release, and accompany her on the journey to their town of General Mamerto Natividad in Nueva Ecija.

blocks.caption: Rappler Talk: Mary Jane Veloso, a free woman

blocks.text: Before returning home, Veloso and her family attended Mass at the Siena College Chapel in Quezon City on Saturday morning. She called her freedom a blessing from the Lord, one that she has fervently prayed for all these years.

“Nagpapasalamat ako sa ating Poong Maykapal. Alam ko lahat ng nangyari sa akin na kabutihan ngayong araw na ‘to ay nagmula sa Kanya,” Veloso, now 41 years old, said in a press conference after the Mass.
(I give thanks to God Almighty. I know that all of the goodness I experienced today came from Him.)

In front of the media, Veloso also recited a poem that she said she was able to put together with help from fellow persons deprived of liberty at the CIW. The poem, titled “Pilipino Ako, Pilipino Ang Wika Ko,” was set to be presented inside the prison facility next week had she not been released.
She also sang the OPM song “Maghintay Ka Lamang,” with her family joining the emotional performance.
It is a meaningful song for Veloso as she used to sing it with her two sons, Mark Daniel Candelaria and Mark Darren Candelaria.
The boys also dedicated the song to their mother on April 23, 2015, days before her scheduled April 29 execution in Indonesia. They were then aged 12 and 6, respectively.
Now, at 23 and 17, the young men are finally reunited with their mother.

Veloso had been granted a last-minute reprieve from execution in Indonesia, but it would take nine more years of detention there before her transfer to the Philippines on December 18, 2024. Appeals for pardon after she was brought back to the country were not immediately granted, so she was detained at the CIW.
By the afternoon of September 26, 2026, Veloso arrived in Nueva Ecija, where a surprise celebration was waiting. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Republic of Ireland news conference delayed before controversial Israel game
articles.summary: The Republic of Ireland delay the pre-match news conference planned for Sunday's Uefa Nations League game against Israel in Hungary - a fixture campaigners have called on them to boycott.

blocks.text: The Republic of Ireland have delayed the pre-match news conference planned for Sunday's Uefa Nations League game against Israel in Hungary - a fixture campaigners have called on them to boycott.
Heimir Hallgrimsson's team are scheduled to meet Israel in Debrecen at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October.
They have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.
Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott.
However, there are also Irish supporters, perhaps less vocal, who have always believed that the match should be played with supporters in attendance.

Following Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo, midfielder Jason Knight opined he didn't think "the game should be going ahead", while winger Chiedozie Ogbene urged the public to not "put the pressure on us" regarding their approach to the scheduled game.
Hallgrimsson and a player were scheduled to meet the media at 09:15 BST (10.15 local time), before training, but the conference was delayed shortly beforehand.
A Uefa official entered the room to inform waiting media teams that the press conference was postponed until after training, which would have been about 11:30 BST (12.30 local time).

But shortly afterwards, the Uefa official returned to the media room to announce that the Republic of Ireland's training session had also been postponed, with no time given for when it might take place. There is also no confirmed time for the news conference.
The fixture has been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.
A team meeting took place on Friday for players to air their views on Sunday's game and the return fixture in Serbia.

The players were expected to release a statement at Saturday's news conference, but the delay has added further uncertainty, with some reports of at least one player wishing to withdraw from the squad.
It has since emerged the news conference, scheduled to take place at the stadium, is now set to be staged at the team hotel, with Uefa unable to provide information regarding the delay.
The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

articles.title: South Korea's gender pay gap grows as women get older
articles.summary: A new report shows how in South Korea, women on average earn less and have fewer employment opportunities throughout their lives.

image.caption: Caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work. Image: DW

blocks.text: At 27, a woman in South Korea earns 8% less than male peers. By her late 50s, she earns 50% less. This is according to government wage data published in a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report.

South Korea is a global technology and industrial powerhouse, but its gender pay gap has remained the highest in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since comparable records began in 1992.
"The gender division of labor inside the home leads directly to a gender division of labor in the labor market," Min Hee Kim, a Korean activist for women labor struggles, told DW.

The problem, she argues, is not simply that women are paid less than men. As women age, the kinds of work available to them narrows and the consequences of lower pay, career breaks and precarious jobs accumulate.
For the report, "Too Old and a Woman," HRW interviewed 41 South Korean women aged 28 to 87 about their working lives.
Structural barriers to women's careers

Discrimination has changed form rather than disappeared, Kim said. Until the 1980s, it was legal for employers to fire women simply for getting married, a practice known as "marriage-based dismissal," where employers assumed a married woman would soon leave to raise children anyway.

Today, "it is difficult to openly say, 'We won't hire you because you're a woman,'" Kim added. But caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work.
According to the HRW report, women's university attainment has passed men's since the 1980s. Higher education would suggest equal opportunity after graduation, but the job market says otherwise.
One year after graduating, women already earn 22% less than men, according to a 2024 study.
Many women told HRW that after leaving work for marriage or children, chances of returning to the workforce were limited to a handful of jobs such as call centers, cleaning or caregiving.
Women who opt to focus on their career told HRW they hit a glass ceiling at work. Women held 18% of manager jobs in 2024, and only five of 38 senior civil servants were women.
Brains, beauty and barriers: the global job market
Wages peak and drop off
Women's wages peak in their late 30s and then steadily decline, according to Labor Ministry survey data cited by HRW.
South Korea's Gender Ministry told HRW that career interruptions, along with occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive the gap.
J. Mi-sook, 53, told HRW that her three years of experience weren't recognized by her next employer, so she started at entry level on a lower salary.
The longer women spend outside the workforce, the less experience they accumulate on their resumes, which results in less pay and less work stability.

Kim pointed to structural discrimination, a concept from the report that HRW describes as discrimination so embedded in social practices and institutions that even the people harmed by it may not recognize it as a problem.

"When you are alone, it is easy to think, 'It's because I'm not capable enough,' or 'It's because I'm getting older,'" she said. It's only when women who've had similar experiences meet and talk, she added, that they realize, "this wasn't just my problem."
It gets harder as you get older

Park Jae-soon, 61, was forced to retire at 60 from a utility company and now works part-time as a care worker. Her annual income fell from 55 million won ($40,500/€35,600) to 15.6 million won, a 72% drop.
HRW argues the mandatory retirement age and the "peak wage" system, which lets employers cut older workers' pay in the years before retirement, should both be abolished.
According to data cited in the report, women received 53% of men's National Old Age Pension on average in October 2025, a 47% gap.
"I think what is important here is that this is not simply a problem of middle-aged women having difficulty finding jobs," Kim said.

"The work that women have traditionally done inside the home, like cleaning, cooking, caregiving and managing other people's emotions, is classified as 'work suitable for women' when it enters the labor market, and then low wages are assigned to it," she added.
How South Korea's cosmetic industry drives career success
From first paycheck to pension
HRW argues the disadvantage builds stage by stage, from a woman's first paycheck up until her pension.

"Career interruption among women in their 30s is already a pension issue," Kim said. "Part-time work among women in their 40s is a pension issue, and low wages among women in their 50s are already a pension issue," she added.
South Korea's government has said it will pursue a phased increase in the statutory retirement age from 60 to 65.

"This cannot be solved with just one policy. Equal pay for equal work needs to be actually implemented, wage structures need to be transparent, and care needs to be treated as a public responsibility rather than something that is pushed onto individual families and women," Kim said.
The rights activist said the report is an important starting point, but believes its picture is incomplete.

Most interviewees were recruited through civic organizations and largely in Seoul, she noted, while disabled women, migrant workers and others may experience a different combination of age and gender discrimination.

"The important question is not simply, 'How much discrimination do women face?'" she said. "It is which women, in what positions, become increasingly distanced from which resources and rights as they grow older."

articles.title: At Eurovision Asia, Carmelle steps onto her biggest stage yet
articles.summary: 'Gusto ko na makilala ako as someone na galing ng Pilipinas na magaling. Kahit papano, siguro mag-open din ‘yun ng door na mas makilala ‘yung ibang artist din na magagaling dito sa Pilipinas,' says…

blocks.text: If you had tuned in to the Philippines’ selection night for Eurovision Asia, Carmelle Collado’s performance should have caught your eye from the get-go.

The moment the lights came on, the young singer had sprung into action — readily wielding her vocals alongside the kulintang and the kubing that had echoed throughout the entire theater. She had hit all the high notes even as she danced across the large stage, and had switched things up toward the end by spitting bars, all while keeping her composure steady as ever.

Her track of the night was “Sobra-sobra,” composed by Mat Olavides and Nica del Rosario, and it was a fitting anthem about refusing to box yourself into external expectations just because you appear to be “too much.”

It was a performance that was distinctly Filipino, yet fit for a global platform like Eurovision Asia. For ABS-CBN Music creatives, content and operations head Jonathan Manalo, then, it had been a no-brainer for Carmelle to be chosen to raise the Philippine flag in the upcoming singing competition.

“We also felt that she has the potential to represent the Philippines beyond the competition itself. She has the discipline and openness to grow, and she understands that representing the country is not just about delivering a performance. It is also about carrying the Filipino identity and musicality onto an international stage,” Manalo told Rappler.
Carmelle’s star power, however, had shone through even before Eurovision Asia came into the picture.

Carmelle was barely three years old when she learned to sing a full song on her own. The people around her, though, would often tell her that she could already hold a note at just two. Before long, she would go on to dominate the intermission numbers they would have at school assemblies, and would establish a command of the mic that just felt natural.

“Nakuha ko ‘yung pagkanta ko sa mother’s side ko,” she beamed as she shared the story she’s likely told a thousand times before. “‘Yung lola ko, nagko-compete siya before kasi taga-Bicol kami. Sa Iriga ‘yung school niya, and then nakakalaban niya si Miss Nora Aunor doon.”
(I got my singing chops from my mother’s side. My grandmother used to enter singing competitions because we’re from Bicol. Her school was in Iriga, and she would go head to head with Nora Aunor.)

It wouldn’t take long for the Pinoy Big Brother Celebrity Collab Edition 2.0 alum to set her sights on platforms outside her hometown. In 2019, she made headlines as the young Bicolana who had impressively earned seven gold medals at the World Championships of Performing Arts (WCOPA) in California.

Things would only get better for the fast-rising star from there. In the same year, she joined The Voice Kids under Coach Bamboo’s team and eventually notched a first runner-up finish. Tawag ng Tanghalan: School Showdown would later become her playground in 2025, and would see her emerge as the show’s grand champion.

blocks.caption: At Eurovision Asia, Carmelle steps onto her biggest stage yet

blocks.text: “Carmelle has always had a very strong musical instinct. She listens, she learns, and she knows how to make a song her own. But I think what really sets her apart is her hunger to keep improving,” Manalo said.

“She has been exposed to competition from a young age, but she never became defined by the competition. She has continued to develop her own identity as an artist. That ability to grow without losing who she is has allowed her to keep moving forward.”
And when it finally came time for her to explore her shot at making history as the Philippines’ first-ever representative to Eurovision Asia, she stayed true to that.

Every time Carmelle enters a competition, she dives into it with the goal of putting on a good show. Winning is merely a bonus. That’s the mindset she has operated on for as long as she could remember, and ironically, it’s exactly what gets her to the top of the podium.

“Kasi kapag inisip mo na competition, makikita mo na sobrang kinakabahan ka. But then ako, sa buong journey ko ng Eurovision, actually, puro nga ako laro eh, hanggang sa nagseryoso. Siguro nagseryoso na lang ako noong time na magpa-perform na ako, parang in-game na ako. Tapos after nung pagtapak ko ng stage, wala na, naglaro na naman si bakla,” she quipped.

(When you think of it as a competition, your anxiety will show. But for me, throughout my whole Eurovision journey, I just remained carefree until I had to get serious. I think I only started to take things seriously when I was about to perform on stage, like I was in-game. After I stepped off the stage, I went back to playing.)

Whether or not she’s on the competition floor, Carmelle’s friends and supporters all know that she moves through life with big smiles and joyous laughter. It’s highly unlikely that the 19-year-old would go a day without cracking a joke or two. As a seasoned performer, she argues that it’s her way of getting rid of the nerves that would otherwise consume her.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by CARMELLE (@carmelle_lite)

Carefree as she is, Carmelle is no stranger to self-doubt. When she had first heard the demo for “Sobra-sobra” and learned that it was composed by hitmakers Olavides and Del Rosario, she had questioned whether she could do justice to their song.

But it was also through Olavides and Del Rosario themselves that she learned to overcome these thoughts. The two producers would often reassure the young singer that it was normal to make mistakes along the way, and that all she had to do was enjoy the process.

Still, as the second-to-the-last performer on the Eurovision Philippines selection night, silent nerves had washed over Carmelle as she watched her competitors take the stage one by one. But when it was finally her turn to sing “Sobra-sobra,” all she remembered in the moments leading up to her big number was surrendering it all to God.
“Backstage pa lang, before magstart, kinakabahan talaga ako. Hindi mo na ako makausap (Backstage, before it started, I was already super nervous. Nobody could speak to me),” she admitted.

But Carmelle has a way of completely transforming herself once the music begins to play. She is fierce, and becomes laser-focused on delivering the best performance she can. This is something audiences had witnessed at the Eurovision Philippines selection night.

“Once na tumapak na ako sa stage or nakita na ako ng maraming tao, kinakalimutan ko na ‘yung side ni Carmelle na kalog. Like, performance level na ‘to. Pop star duty na ‘yung aatakihin natin ngayon. Pero after ng performance, kalog-kalog na naman tayo,” she shared.

(Once I step on stage or I see that many people are watching me, I forget the silly side of myself. Like, this is performance-level already. I have to get into my pop star duty. But after the performance, I go back to being quirky.)

After Carmelle had sung the first line of “Sobra-sobra,” she had completely forgotten that it was a competition in the first place. One of her biggest strengths, she told Rappler, is her ability to forget about all the emotions that were previously weighing her down once she faces the crowd.

“Nawawala yung kaba. More on nag-enjoy na lang ako. Hindi ko na naiisip na competition siya. Like, ‘Okay, nag-perform ako.’ Kailangan ang goal lang is makapag-perform ako nang maayos at saka i-prove sa kanila na magaling ako, magaling kaming lahat,” she explained.

(The nervousness goes away. I just enjoy it. I don’t think about it as a competition. Like, ‘Okay, I performed.’ My goal is just to perform properly and prove to everyone that I’m good, that we’re all good.)
With Eurovision Asia just a few months away, there’s only one thing Carmelle wants people to remember about her when they watch her in Bangkok: that she is good at what she does.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mark Kingson Qua (@mkqua)

“‘Yung audience din kasi ng Eurovision, pangmalawakan na siya. So, gusto ko na makilala ako as someone na galing ng Pilipinas na magaling. Kahit papano, siguro mag-open din ‘yun ng door na mas makilala ‘yung ibang artist din na magagaling dito sa Pilipinas,” she said.

(The audience of Eurovision is huge. So, I want people to know me as someone from the Philippines who is talented. In one way or another, I also hope it opens doors for even more talented Filipino artists to be recognized, too.) – Rappler.com
Eurovision Asia 2026 is set to take place on November 14 in Bangkok, Thailand.

articles.title: Teodoro says Marcos ordered probe into 'nefarious' foreign activities in PH
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has ordered an investigation into “nefarious” foreign activities in the Philippines, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said Saturday.

blocks.text: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has ordered an investigation into “nefarious” foreign activities in the Philippines, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said Saturday.

“President Marcos has instructed our intelligence agencies and law enforcement agencies to conduct evidence-based operations against these forms of nefarious activities,” Teodoro said at the Saturday News Forum.

Teodoro made the statement as he discussed various illegal activities allegedly involving Chinese nationals, citing the case of dismissed Bamban, Tarlac Mayor Alice Guo and the proliferation of substandard steel plants.

Guo, also known as Guo Hua Ping, was elected mayor of Bamban in 2022 but was later found to have used fraudulent birth documents. She has also faced allegations of links to Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) and foreign interests.
Teodoro also cited the case of a mayor in the United States who was reportedly discovered to be an agent for China.
He said there were signs linking Guo to Chinese businessman Tony Yang, the brother of former presidential adviser Michael Yang.

“With the discovery of Alice Guo as a fake Filipino, and Tony Yang as an admitted fake Filipino... who, by the way, there is some information to show that they are, have some relationship with each other and internationally, as part of an international cabal,” Teodoro said.
Teodoro also alleged that Tony Yang had collaborators in Cambodia who were part of the same gang as individuals behind a large-scale money laundering scheme in Singapore.
POGOs and steel plants
The massive POGO hub established in Bamban, Tarlac, was built within two years during the COVID-19 pandemic, with almost all of its materials and workers imported from abroad, Teodoro said.

“Kung nakapasok na ganun kabilis, ganun kadaming materyales, ganun kadaming tao, pandemic, ano pa kaya yung droga? Ano pa kaya yung ibang mga bagay? Yun ang dapat examine natin, hindi lang si Alice Guo, pero yung buong support system niya. Mangyayari na yan sa isang pribadong indibidwal lamang na sarado ang buong mundo noon? Tingin ko hindi,” Teodoro said.

(If they were able to enter that fast, with that many materials, that many people, during the pandemic, what about drugs? What about other things? That is what we must examine, not just Alice Guo, but her entire support system. Can that be done by one private individual while the world was closed? I think not.)
“At ano pinaggagawa doon? Puro krimen ang nangyari,” he added.
(And what did they do there? A lot of crime happened.)
Apart from Guo and POGOs, Teodoro said the proliferation of substandard steel plants also posed a problem because of their potential impact on the economy.
He cited the Tony Yang-linked Sanjia Steel Corp. in Misamis Oriental as an example of what he described as China’s growing economic influence in the Philippines.

Authorities raided the Sanjia facility in May, resulting in the arrest of 69 Chinese nationals. The government has said the workers were undocumented and that the operation uncovered potentially hazardous materials.

“We have seen the proliferation of substandard steel plants, which serves as a barrier of entry to the market by underpricing the commodity and selling unsafe foundational structures for construction and other matters, and contaminated too by the way,” Teodoro said.

“What does this do? You need a steel industry, you need a bona fide steel industry to manufacture, especially for your defense. Can you imagine using substandard steel for vessels which are... contaminated? You can’t do that,” he added.

“The objective here, really, obviously, is to create a culture of dependence on China, which continues to feed the consumer-consumption-led economy of the Philippines by flooding us with cheap retail goods while preventing us from developing our core industries which we need for resilience,” Teodoro said.
Philippines-China ties
Philippines-China diplomatic relations have become more strained during the Marcos administration amid renewed tensions over the West Philippine Sea.
Teodoro, however, said previous administrations had already attempted to improve ties with China but that Beijing continued to exert pressure on Philippine interests.
He cited Beijing’s 1995 claim that it was building a shelter for Chinese fishermen on Mischief Reef as an example.
But now, it is a military base, Teodoro said.
Teodoro also warned that China was attempting to create a “Sinocentric” world.

While he said he did not want to foster a culture of sinophobia in the Philippines, the defense chief argued that any such sentiment would be a consequence of the actions of the Chinese Communist Party. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: One dead and five missing after explosion destroys building close to Acropolis in Athens
articles.summary: Local media report the property included a holiday rental, with US tourists and a UK national among the missing.

blocks.text: At least one person has died and five more are missing after an explosion destroyed a building in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis, with local media reporting the building housed a holiday rental.
Four American tourists, one British national and a Greek national are said to the people involved - though that has not been confirmed by authorities.
Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through the rubble, with a gas leak suspected as the cause of the blast.
The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with the search ongoing.
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office.

articles.title: Trump reportedly rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Tehran awaits official response to plan, but US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms

Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of…

blocks.text: Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East war as Donald Trump was reported to have rejected the deal.

Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the UN general assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted ⁠to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could ⁠reopen the strategic waterway and put an end ​to hostilities in the region within seven days.

But the US president is sceptical and has told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed US officials.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive”.

Iran has offered to reopen the strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear programme in seven days if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observed a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council on Friday, saying the country would also restart stalled talks with the US on Iran’s nuclear programme. “The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said.

Araghchi said the initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, and the strait would be open on the sixth day. “And on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” he said, referring to the nuclear programme.
“If there is seriousness on the US side to ⁠come to a deal and reopen the strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araqchi said.

The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the strait, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and taken a toll on the global economy.

Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons“.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump during his address to the UN general assembly. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.

Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.

Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict, which has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and drawn in regional and world powers.
Early on Saturday, Yemen’s ⁠Saudi-led ⁠coalition said ⁠it ​intercepted ‌two ‌drones ‌launched by the Iran-backed ‌Houthis towards ​the ⁠Saudi ​capital, Riyadh.

Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq have been blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. All the while, Iranian-backed Hezbollah has been engaged with Israeli forces in Lebanon.
With Reuters and AP

articles.title: Deadly blast rips through Athens building, near Acropolis
articles.summary: Several foreign tourists remain missing after an explosion brought down a building in Athens' tourist area of Plaka, with the city's mayor calling it an "incredible disaster."

image.caption: Local media reported several Americans were staying in the collapsed buildingImage: Aristidis Vafeiadakis/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rescuers have recovered the body of a young woman following a building collapse in Plaka, in central Athens, a Greek fire brigade official said Saturday.
The building was brought down by a large blast which injured three other people and damaged shops and cars near the site.
"The damage extends along the entire street as well as the street behind the building," said Athens Mayor Haris Doukas. "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
Several people, believed to be foreign nationals, remain missing.
On Saturday, Greek news agency ANA reported that the victim whose body was retrieved was an American tourist, sharing the holiday rental with her husband and another couple.
Cause of the blast still uncertain
Authorities suspect a gas leak caused the Friday blast, but the sequence of events was not immediately clear.
"Something went terribly wrong," Doukas said.
Local media reported the missing people included a Briton and a Greek woman who lived on the second floor, and four American tourists staying on the first floor.
While their nationalities have not been officially confirmed, a police official said the group of tourists had been expected to check in for a flight from Athens on early Friday afternoon.
Excavators on the scene

Rescuers were using sniffer dogs and thermal cameras to search for possible survivors. According to ANA, dozens of firefighters and six vehicles have been deployed to help with the search, including two specialized rescue vehicles.
Excavators were also deployed to clear the rubble, according to photos from the scene.
Plaka is close to many Athens most visited sites, including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus.
