articles.title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
articles.summary: Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC "constructive discussions" were taking place through mediators.

blocks.text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.
Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.
"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.

Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.
"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.
He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".
"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.
A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".
The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief.
It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements.
But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.

The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.
Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz.

Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters.
However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula.

The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.

articles.title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
articles.summary: Roelf Meyer tells the BBC that being a white Afrikaner gives him legitimacy to challenge Trump's claim of a genocide.
articles.byline: Ione Wells, Mayeni Jones, Ed Habershon

blocks.text: South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.

Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.

In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.

In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.

"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.

The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.

Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.

Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".

Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.

Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.

But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

articles.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
articles.summary: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.

blocks.text: A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.
But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.
It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.
Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.
A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.
A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.
A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.
Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.
And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.
That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.
In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).
But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.
It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.
Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.
Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.

Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag.

"I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."
Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.
He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.
And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success.
This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.
But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.
Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.
It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.
And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.
While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).

Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.
Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.
Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

articles.title: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
articles.summary: Current and former agents speak to the BBC about the devastating impact of the FBI hack.

blocks.text: Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce.
"This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues.
The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes.
The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met.
Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated.
"One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker.
"They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases."

Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.
The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.
The FBI has not responded to requests for comment.
However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".
He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.

"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.
ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.
The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.
The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.
The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".
Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.

Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.
"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.
There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.
Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen.
The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group.
One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach.
There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened.
The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site.
Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them.
"The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me.
He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate.

articles.title: OpenAI investigating 'dozens' of instances of agents acting improperly
articles.summary: OpenAI agents tried to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through extreme means that sometimes curbed security controls, the company said.

blocks.text: OpenAI said Friday it had alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been impacted by its AI agents acting improperly.
OpenAI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through sometimes extreme means, the company said.

While some of the activity was simply due to the tools working to find "authoritative sources of public information," some went beyond that. Like an AI agent taking and transferring data when it should not have, OpenAI said.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had allowed OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted, "This is not an appropriate use of this data".
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported these issues.

OpenAI also indicated on Friday that its software may have circumvented certain security controls of the sites impacted - though it doesn't necessarily mean each incident led to a significant security breach.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning. Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address," the company said.

OpenAI said it came across the incidents during an investigation that started after it learned that its AI models had hacked the AI platform Hugging Face, an incident that was revealed publicly last month.

The disclosures on Friday comes just days after Australian's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said OpenAI had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme, Medicare.

articles.title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
articles.summary:
Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada

The CEO of a

blocks.text: The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.

Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.

Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.

As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.

“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.

After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.

“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.

Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.summary: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.

blocks.text: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus Tymann
Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range
ByAbraham Utama
BBC Indonesia
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

blocks.caption: Map and satellite image showing rapidly shrinking glaciers around Puncak Jaya in Indonesia's Papua region. Labels mark nearby peaks including Sumantri, Ngga Pulu and Carstensz East, with a callout noting that glaciers near the peaks are disappearing. An inset map locates Papua on the island of Ne…

blocks.text: "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936

blocks.text: The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936
Proof of a warming planet

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems

blocks.text: Image source, Marie Šabacká
Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems
A spiritual anchor
At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.
The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".

"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."
According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.
Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.

"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe

blocks.text: The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe
For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.
The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.
Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.

Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.
The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.

"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."

blocks.caption: Image caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue

blocks.text: This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue
As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.
Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.
From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."
Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.
"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.
Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.
"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

articles.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
articles.summary: Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

image.caption: The civil war between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis has escalated sharply amid the Iran war Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.
The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.
What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.
He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.
Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.
"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?
Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.
The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.

articles.title: Lula or Bolsonaro as president? Brazil gears up to vote
articles.summary: Brazilians go to the polls on October 4. The front-runners are multilateralist incumbent Lula da Silva and former President Jair Bolsonaro's son, Flavio, who wants to bring Brazil closer to the US…

image.caption: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (seen at left and right) is facing off with Flavio Bolsonaro (center)Image: Sergio Lima/AFP

blocks.text: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva spoke in no uncertain terms at the opening of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday in New York: "Brazil does not belong in anyone's backyard," the Brazilian president said. His comment was directed at his US counterpart Donald Trump, despite Trump not being in attendance.

The US president has repeatedly interfered with Brazilian domestic politics, siding with former President Jair Messias Bolsonaro and the far-right opposition. In July, Trump imposed sanctions on a judge who found Bolsonaro guilty of attempting a coup and sentenced him to 27 years in jail. Washington only lifted the sanctions after negotiating with Lula.
Bolsonaro's eldest son Flavio is Lula's biggest challenger in the upcoming presidential election on October 4, and polls currently show the two of them to be neck and neck in a potential runoff.

The election in the world's fifth largest country is drawing a great deal of international attention. Brazil is an agricultural giant and very rich in natural resources — boasting rare earth elements, vast water resources and enormous crude oil reserves.
Brazil one of South America's last bastions of the left

Lula is the "last man standing" of the South American left, while Flavio Bolsonaro is part of an increasingly strong far-right camp. Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia all have governments that are sympathetic to Trump. And since January, Venezuela has been what some describe as a US protectorate.

blocks.caption: Lula advocates for multilateralist diplomacy and good international relations with all countriesImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Foreign policy hasn't played a big role in the campaign, but this election will nonetheless decide whether Brazil moves closer to Trump's US. Washington is seeking economic and military dominance in South America through the Shield of the Americas initiative, focused on combating violent cartels. After his military intervention in Venezuela, Trump is now exerting economic pressure on Mexico and Cuba. At the same time, he is trying to counter Chinese influence in the region.
For his part, Lula is an advocate of multilateralist diplomacy, wanting Brazil to engage in dialogue and trade with everybody. China has long been Brazil's most important trading partner.

Flavio Bolsonaro favors a conservative alliance with the US and other right-wing states. But for Leonardo Paz from the Brazilian Fundacao Getulio Vargas think tank, a Bolsonaro victory would not necessarily automatically mean better relations with the US. He told DW that Lula had established a largely normal relationship with Trump — both are 80 years old — despite some initial friction. The two leaders got along well, said Paz, even if Lula has not succumbed to Trump's pressure.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

Paz did admit that if Bolsonaro won, the 45-year-old would be more likely to accommodate Trump, pointing out that his father Jair had made far-reaching concessions to the US when he was president. During Jair Bolsonaro's time in office from 2019 to 2023, Brazil agreed to forgo its "developing country status" in World Trade Organization negotiations in exchange for a mere promise that the US would back its bid to become a member of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Trump also said he was considering giving Brazil NATO "privileges." Neither promise came to anything.

"While relations with the US would continue as they are with Lula, it is completely unclear what a Flavio Bolsonaro presidency would mean," Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat and minister, told DW. "Lula has prestige in foreign policy, while Bolsonaro is completely inexperienced."
Would Brazil pull out of BRICS?

A victory for Bolsonaro would likely jeopardize Brazil's role in BRICS, the alliance that comprises Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and five other states. Bolsonaro has said that one of his first acts would be to review whether Brazil should stay in the alliance, arguing that BRICS only serves to provoke the US. He has also spoken out against China's efforts to reduce the global dominance of the US dollar.

It's hard to tell how serious such intentions are, considering the importance of economic ties between China and Brazil. Javier Milei, Argentina's current president, also engaged in harsh rhetoric against China before he came to power, but quickly adopted a more conciliatory tone once in office to not jeopardize Chinese loans.
"Political relations with China would likely cool, but I wouldn't expect any substantial changes in economic and commercial relations," predicted Ricupero in case of a Bolsonaro victory.

Paz agreed that Flavio Bolsonaro was unlikely to take an extremely aggressive stance toward China in case of victory. He explained that, like Milei, Jair Bolsonaro had engaged in some sharp rhetoric against Beijing at the beginning of his term but had quickly softened his tone, given the fact that Brazil's agricultural sector in particular is so dependent on China.

Paz pointed out that the Bolsonaro family enjoyed most support in Brazil's rural regions, which made good money with China. "The unknown factor with Flavio Bolsonaro is how much pressure the US would exert so that Brazil distanced itself from China and to what extent he would yield to the pressure," said Paz.

blocks.caption: If he wins, Flavio Bolsonaro is expected to dismantle policies that protect the environment Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazil not likely to become major world player

Paz said that despite possessing enormous natural resources that are important to the global economy, Brazil would likely remain a minor player on the world stage as it had neither the economic strength to provide financial aid to other countries nor the military strength to help resolve conflicts. "This severely limits Brazil's ability to act," he said.

But Brazil could continue to be a major protagonist in the Global South, he said, as it is under Lula. "This is particularly evident in the international debate on global governance, in which Brazil raises issues such as new trading conditions, climate policy and development," he said.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro supporters, seen here with a Trump inflatable at a rally on September 7, favor a Brazil that is close to Trump's US Image: Alexandre Meneghini/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ricupero said Lula carried particular weight in foreign policy, especially regarding the environment and climate change. "His commitment to addressing ecological challenges was clear from his choice of [leading environmentalist] Marina Silva as environment minister," he said.

The former diplomat said he feared Flavio Bolsonaro would repeat the mistakes of his father, and this was one of the reasons the election was drawing such attention from around the world. He pointed out that Brazil had become more isolated after Jair Bolsonaro dismantled major environmental policies, adding that relations with the European Union had particularly suffered and negotiations on a trade agreement between Mercosur and the bloc had been put on hold. The deal was finally signed early this year.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?
articles.summary: Kratom, found during an investigation into the deaths of two college students, has been sold in the US for around a decade.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBrandon Drenon and Madeline Halpert
Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain.
He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away.
"It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function.
"I just don't know what I'd do without it."
Kratom - an herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over-the-counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.

This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption.

For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.
Here's what we know about it:
What is kratom?
Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.
It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea.
As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016.
"That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University.
In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said.
It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops.
Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated.

"There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it."
What is kratom used for?
Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression.
In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained.
Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl.
Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine.
What are the effects and how dangerous is it?
"It's almost like taking a narcotic," Speights said. "At higher doses, it can create more euphoria and give you more of a general high."
Hallucinations are possible, too.
The higher doses also pose greater risk for adverse side effects.
That includes central nervous system (CNS) depression - which is "where the deaths come in," Speights said.
CNS can result in cardiovascular collapse and loss of breathing.
Withdrawal symptoms and addiction are also risks, said Jana Wu, director of clinical integration at the addiction treatment centre Mountainside.
"It affects marriages, relationships," she said. "I've seen people lose jobs, spend thousands of dollars a month on it."
Because it's easy to develop a high tolerance to the herb, users may need to take an increasing amount to achieve the same effect over time.
"I've worked with people that were taking like up to 20 pills a day," Wu said.
Experts told the BBC that the biggest dangers come from the fact that kratom is not federally regulated.
"Is there a safe dose?" Speights said. "My answer is going to be no because - I'm going to go back to this - we don't know what's in it."
Is kratom legal?
Kratom is banned in 11 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin.
Massachusetts was the last state to make it illegal, issuing a temporary emergency order in August.
Ten years earlier, the US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) had moved to classify kratom as a Schedule 1, the most dangerous level for drugs, calling it "an imminent hazard to public safety".
But the effort failed a few months later, after the justice department said it received "numerous comments from members of the public challenging" the attempt.
That leaves states to take action, like Arizona, which recently sued a company selling kratom beverage products.
Groups opposed to kratom want states to do more, saying "gas-station drugs are poisoning our communities".
Pro-kratom groups like the American Kratom Association are pushing for bans against synthetics "posing as natural kratom".
Internationally, kratom is banned in the UK. In Europe, the laws vary by country.
In Malaysia, where the kratom tree is native, consumption and sale are banned under the Poisons Act of 1952.

articles.title: Why an international arrest warrant didn't stop Netanyahu's US trip
articles.summary: The BBC's Nada Tawfik explains why Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu was not arrested after speaking at the UN, despite an ICC arrest warrant.

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly on 24 September. His speech occurred while an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes is in effect. The BBC's Nada Tawfik explains why Netanyahu was not arrested after speaking at the UN General Assembly.
Related topics

articles.title: Zelensky says Russia has widened attacks to hit Ukraine's data centres
articles.summary: Such strikes aim to disrupt "people's ability to stay connected, study, work", says Ukraine's president.

blocks.text: President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people.
"All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said.

On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said the teenager was an Israeli citizen.
Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes. Some firms are already transferring data from damaged servers abroad.

In the north-western city Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv".

In a post on social media on Friday, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers - for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target.
"It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror."
On Wednesday, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres.

"Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said.

Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs.
But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access".

The latest data centre hit by Russia is run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after Friday's daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites".
Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence.
Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC.

The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi.
In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure - seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches.
Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In a separate development on Friday, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday.
In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented.
The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.
In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have warned Russia may be preparing hybrid attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.
Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

articles.title: Two arrested after people seen mysteriously emerging from various New York City sewers
articles.summary: The city has seen a string of incidents in which people have climbed out of manholes late at night.

blocks.text: New York officials arrested two of three men who they said were seen emerging from a manhole, exiting the city's underground sewer system on Wednesday.
The New York Police Department (NYPD) arrested 26-year-old Kevin Rodriguez and 25-year-old Samuel Reveron on charges of conspiracy and trespassing.
Three men were seen exiting a manhole near the hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was reportedly expected to stay for the United Nations General Assembly.
In a statement to the BBC, the NYPD said it had seen a number of incidents involving people going into the sewer system to look for valuables and scrap metal after a storm.

"This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the U.N. General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners," the police department said in a statement.

Rodriguez and Reveron, both from Queens, were arrested on Thursday. They allegedly fled the scene after climbing out of the manhole when officers were called around 4:30 EST (9:30 BST) on Wednesday, police said.
During a hearing on Friday morning, the two men pleaded not guilty and were released from custody, according to court records.
The arrests follow a string of incidents in which people were seen emerging from pavement manholes in different parts of the city in recent months.

In August, surveillance footage showed a person coming out of a manhole in Queens early in the morning. The same month, the NYPD said it was investigating three people wearing overalls and headlamps seen climbing out of a manhole near Penn Station.
In May, a group of people were captured on surveillance footage shifting a manhole cover and climbing down into the sewer in South Brooklyn.
Going into the New York sewer system is both illegal and dangerous, officials have said, cautioning that there is a risk of toxic gases and flooding in a confined space.
"For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall," the city's Department of Environmental Protection previously told the BBC.
This year, a woman died after she opened her car door and accidentally fell into an open manhole in Midtown Manhattan.

articles.title: Protests erupt as Netanyahu gives inflammatory UN speech - The Latest
articles.summary: More than 100 people were arrested at large protests against the Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the UN general assembly. Susan Sarandon, Chelsea Manning and Caleb Hearon…
articles.byline: Presented by Lucy Hough with Devika Bhat; produced by Angus Neale; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin; executive producer Zoe Hitch

blocks.text: More than 100 people were arrested at large protests against the Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the UN general assembly. Susan Sarandon, Chelsea Manning and Caleb Hearon were among the famous faces arrested. Inside the assembly hall, Netanyahu faced a mass walkout as he took to the stage. Then, in an inflammatory address, he claimed Israel’s war in Gaza was the ‘opposite of a genocide’ and labelled the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, antisemitic. articles.title: Supreme Court revives controversial US data system for citizenship checks
articles.summary: The system uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to filter alleged non-citizen voting.

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal voter database, which uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to filter alleged non-citizen voting.
Critics warn the ruling could lead to valid voters being removed from electoral rolls.
The ruling marks a victory for the Trump administration as it seeks to clamp down on allegations of non-citizen voting.

The three liberal-leaning liberals on the Supreme Court dissented from the decision, with the other six conservative justices supporting it. In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.
The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.

The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits. But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using social security numbers.

In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote."
A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.

articles.title: Alberta’s ‘rat patrol’ ramps up operations as vermin makes inroads in province
articles.summary:
‘Rat-free’ Canadian province recently took a verminous hit when a dead rodent turned up in town of Bowden

For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common…

blocks.text: For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common with Antarctica and the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats.

But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of a dead rat and called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate.
“If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.”
Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found.

But as global temperatures increase, rat numbers have surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years.
Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all.
“Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide.

It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation.

In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south.
In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats.

The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found; made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents.
Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats.
But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice.

Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”

articles.title: Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list
articles.summary:
Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media

The organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had…

blocks.text: The organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.

The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.
Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.

blocks.caption: The novel on display inside a bookstore in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: Allegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.

An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.
Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.
Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”
He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”

blocks.caption: Orélien at Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque this week. Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The author of the anonymous X account was later identified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaro as one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokism” on film and TV.
On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.

On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged “caution” over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.

Libération alleged in an article that the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.
after newsletter promotion

In its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.
“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”

In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”
The Canada-based publisher said it was important not to “jump to conclusions”, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”

Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.

Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me”, adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.
The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.

articles.title: Thousands turn out to greet Pope in France
articles.summary: The BBC's Hugh Schofield looks at why the visit is met with enthusiasm the Church attributes to growing spirituality among the French.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in France for his four-day visit, where he has delivered an address ahead of a giant Mass to be attended by more than half a million people in central Paris.
President Emmanuel Macron greeted the Pope at Orly airport, before he spoke at the Élysée Palace on geopolitical issues and artificial intelligence (AI).
The BBC's Paris correpondent Hugh Schofield looks at why the visit is met with enthusiasm the Church attributes to growing spirituality among the French.

articles.title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
articles.summary:
Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?

Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen…

blocks.text: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.

In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.

Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.
Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.

The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.

“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.

blocks.caption: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says the new deal contains the elements of June’s memorandum of understanding. Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images

blocks.text: In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US will have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver lifting sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.

On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations will start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the Iranian stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.

Those talks could, of course, then take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.
Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – has every reason not to negotiate with the US.

In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, with Witkoff saying the talks had been “productive and good”, only for Iran to be bombed by the US the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he were to do that, a deal would be feasible.

It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.

blocks.caption: Is Trump prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterm elections? Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that he says, with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgement he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran, after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.

Pezeshkian – who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, who was sitting to his right – admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.

He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei was completely healthy, he claimed – a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain what, apart from security, led Khamenei to not even issue a voice recording, photograph, let alone a video, as proof of life.

articles.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
articles.summary: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

image.caption: More than 70% of Georgians still support the country's accession to the European Union. Protesters are still fighting for a better futureImage: Sébastien Canaud/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I personally don't feel safe as a citizen in my country and as a person who has worked for independent media for a long time," Georgian media expert and advocate for press freedom Nino Robakidze told DW. Her activism with international civil society groups has made her a target in her home country.

Similarly, Georgian journalists are currently facing "physical threats, digital threats, psychological threats. And there is also financial and legal pressure around their media organizations," she reported.

Robakidze was one of the participants at DW's panel discussion "Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia," held on Thursday in Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.

Host Jochen Rosenkranz, director of DW's Culture and Sports department, pointed out in his introduction that it had been difficult to find Georgians willing to participate in the panel. Many had refused, saying they feared the repercussions not only for themselves, but also for their friends and family.

"We're all afraid of the intimidation," Georgian-born musician, filmmaker, journalist and cultural organizer Marika Lapauri-Burk explained. She nevertheless agreed to take part in the discussion, alongside Nino Robakidze and journalist Juri Rescheto, head of DW's Riga bureau.

blocks.caption: Jochen Rosenkranz, Marika Lapauri-Burk, Nino Robakidze and Juri Rescheto at the DW discussion panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Lapauri-Burk added that the government had become increasingly creative in its arbitrary reasons to detain those with critical voices.
Local civil society groups and human rights organizations estimate that from 90 to over 100 political dissidents and protesters are currently imprisoned or in pre-trial detention.
Russian influence impacting democratization efforts
Once thought of as a leading democracy of the Caucasus region, Georgia is undergoing a rapid transition toward authoritarianism under the Georgian Dream (GD) party, in power now since 2012.

The party originally declared itself pro-European, but in recent years has sought more overtly to align with Russia. The party gained an increased majority in a contested October 2024 parliamentary election.

A month later, the GD announced the suspension of EU accession negotiations until 2028, despite a substantial majority of Georgians strongly favoring European integration. Halting the talks ignited demonstrations across the country as the government increasingly aligned its policies with Moscow.
Demonstrators try to storm Georgia's presidential palace

But the transformation could be felt years before the election: "The real pressure on independent media and professional journalists escalated after the Russia's unprovoked invasion in Ukraine," says Robakidze. An important anti-Western campaign followed the invasion, which "had a huge impact on Georgian media environment at large," she added.

The country was also rocked by anti-government protests in 2023-2024 as pro-EU protesters took to the streets. They were pushing back against new, Russian-style "foreign agents" legislation, which required all organizations that received foreign funding to register with the state and comply with extensive reporting requirements.

That came into force in June 2025, and a stricter version has introduced criminal liability and prison sentences of up to five years for individuals and groups who fail to register their activities as being "under foreign influence."

blocks.caption: Nino Robakidze speaking at the panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Culture directly affected by the law

Many independent cultural institutions, festivals, arts organizations and heritage projects are heavily reliant on funding from the European Union, European foundations and international cultural programs.
Critics say the law stigmatizes institutions for their vaguely defined "foreign influence."
The same laws that target activists and journalists threaten the grants, partnerships and institutions that have connected Georgian artists to Europe for decades.

The state agency responsible for enforcing the "foreign agents" law, known as the Anti-Corruption Bureau, uses the law to persecute prominent civil society groups, launching inspections and freezing their bank accounts.
Another law also operates in tandem with the controversial "foreign agent" legislation.

Georgia's anti-LGBTQ law, officially a legislative package entitled "On Family Values and the Protection of Minors," explicitly bans the "popularization" or "propaganda" of same-sex relationships and non-binary gender identities in public spaces, media, education and the arts.
Freedom of expression under threat
Cultural producers are forced to risk choosing between self-censorship, shutting down entirely or facing severe state retaliation.

"The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for critical thinkers — especially artists," explained Juri Rescheto, who notes that many critical thinkers can be found within artistic circles. They are affected "not only in their art but also in their private lives," he added.

Rescheto cited the example of a small gallery he visited in the city of Gori, where protesters' slogans were projected onto a wall as part of an exhibition. It all felt "harmless, really — or so we would say here in the West," the journalist said. Yet the gallery is now facing closure because the city refuses to renew their lease since the action, he added.

blocks.caption: A protest performance by the 'Vaso Abashidze State New Theater' in 2025Image: Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto/picture alliance
